title: Kinetically induced order from mobility-constrained excitations
authors: Aprem P. Joy, Urban F. P. Seifert
abstract: A fascinating feature of strongly correlated systems is that excitations may carry nontrivial quantum numbers under emergent symmetries which, in some cases, may strongly constrain their motion. We show that such constrained excitations can play a central role in driving symmetry-breaking long-range order through a kinetic mechanism: coupling to a local order-parameter field activates the mobility of otherwise constrained excitations, and condensation of the order parameter then enables a large gain in kinetic energy, thereby stabilizing a phase with long-range order. We illustrate this mechanism in two settings: (i) a dimerization instability in a spin chain with a magnetization dipole conservation law, and (ii) itinerant magnetism of electrons in the Kitaev-Kondo model, where charge carriers couple to local moments that form a spin liquid. This mechanism becomes operative whenever a finite density of mobility-constrained excitations is present, either through non-equilibrium preparation or thermal activation. In the latter case, we argue that increasing temperature can, counterintuitively, promote order by enhancing the kinetic-energy gain of thermally activated excitations.
summary: This paper reveals that symmetry-breaking long-range order can emerge kinetically when excitations are initially constrained by symmetries. By coupling the system to an order parameter field, these constraints are lifted, allowing excitations to gain kinetic energy that stabilizes the ordered phase. The mechanism is successfully applied to both spin chains and itinerant magnetism in the Kitaev-Kondo model.
main_problem: The study investigates how kinetic energy gain from excitations, particularly those initially constrained by symmetries, can drive a symmetry-breaking phase transition into a state with long-range order.
main_result: This mechanism is demonstrated in both spin chains (dimerization instability) and the Kitaev-Kondo model, showing that finite density of mobile excitations can stabilize ordered phases, even counterintuitively promoting order at higher temperatures.
method: The analysis employs mean-field theory, perturbation theory in small coupling constants, and free energy functional minimization to track the stability boundaries driven by kinetic energy contributions.
model_or_system: The work analyzes two primary models: (i) a spin chain with dipole conservation coupled to lattice distortions, and (ii) the Kitaev-Kondo model involving itinerant electrons interacting with local moments forming a spin liquid. The Hamiltonian includes terms for hopping, magnetic coupling, and interaction.
key_observables: Dimerization order parameter ($\langle u angle$), spontaneous magnetization ($\vec{m}$), and the critical coupling strength ($g_c$ or $J_{c,0}$) required to induce ordering.
important_parameters: Coupling constants ($g$, $J$), temperature ($T$), excitation gap ($\Delta v$), and density of excitations.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on mean-field approximations for the order parameter fields (e.g., lattice distortion or local magnetization) and perturbative expansions in small coupling strengths.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate how dimerization activates mobility in a spin chain, show vison dispersion upon coupling to a magnetized band, and present phase diagrams mapping kinetic energy gain against order parameters.
paper_structure: The paper develops the general mechanism first, applying it sequentially to two distinct physical realizations: the 1D spin chain instability, followed by the more complex 2D Kitaev-Kondo model analysis involving vison excitations and free energy calculations at finite temperature.
why_interesting: The concept of order being driven by kinetic energy gain rather than purely minimizing potential energy is a powerful general mechanism applicable to many quantum systems, including those studied in AMO physics (e.g., superfluid transitions or Bose-Einstein condensation).
